name: Anyroad
tagline: Drive any road on Earth, built from live map data.
description:
Search for anywhere on the planet, drop in, and drive. There is no built world and no level designer: the road under your wheels is the real road, streamed from OpenStreetMap as you approach it, laid over real elevation so a mountain pass climbs, a coast road falls away, and a crest will launch you if you take it fast enough.

You land on the nearest road facing along it, and from there you go wherever you like — the tarmac is a suggestion, not a track. Steering is quick in town and lazy at speed, hills cost you going up and run away with you coming down, and the handbrake still does what you would hope. Buildings are solid, so watch the corners; hold the brake at a standstill to back out of one, and if a courtyard really has you, one button puts you back on the road.

The verges are not empty. Deer, sheep, boar, geese and the occasional cow graze beside the road and wander across it, and hitting one costs you — damage shows up as cracks spreading across your windscreen rather than as a number in a corner. Turn them off in Settings if you would rather have the roads to yourself.

Other cars use the same roads you do, at whatever that class of road is built for, keeping to their side and slowing for what is in front of them — set the traffic from empty roads to heavy, or turn it off. And you can hear all of it: the engine has a gearbox, the tyres change note when you leave the tarmac for gravel, other cars pass with a doppler, and animals call from wherever they actually are. None of it is a recording — there is no audio in the file, it is all generated as you drive.

Racing needs no server and no accounts. Set a start, drive to a finish, set that, and send the invite link: everyone who opens it lands in the same place on Earth, in the same world, with live cars and a finish board. The host's browser holds the state and nothing touches a game server, because there isn't one.

Every data source is swappable in Settings — elevation, roads, and imagery each name a provider you can change, so a busy or unavailable service is a menu item rather than a dead app. It runs on genuinely open data by default with no key and no account. If you have your own MapTiler key you can switch the ground to satellite imagery; the key lives in GifOS Settings and the app never sees it.

Road geometry is cached on your device so re-driving an area needs no network at all.
